title: Antandros and the shape of Book 3
greek: classemque sub ipsa Antandro et Phrygiae molimur montibus Idae
short: The exiles build their fleet at Antandros under Mount Ida; Book 3 then follows a voyage of false starts (Thrace, Delos, Crete) before the true goal is revealed.
body: Antandros was a town on the Gulf of Adramyttium, south of Troy, below the timber-rich slopes of Mount Ida. Book 3 is Virgil's counterpart to Odysseus' wanderings in Odyssey 9-12, but it is built differently: it is a story of gradual revelation, in which each attempt to settle (Thrace, Crete) fails and each prophecy (Apollo at Delos, the Penates, Celaeno, Helenus) clarifies the destination a little more. It also retraces geography familiar to Romans: the Aegean, western Greece and Sicily. The book has often been judged the least finished of the poem, with inconsistencies in its chronology and prophecies; R. D. Williams' commentary discusses these and the book's place in the poem. Conington's introduction to the book works out its timetable of about seven years.

title: Thrace, land of Mars
greek: terra procul vastis colitur Mavortia campis (Thraces arant), acri quondam regnata Lycurgo
short: Thrace, across the sea from Troy, was the land of Mars (Mavors, an old form of his name) and of King Lycurgus; Aeneas' first city there is named after himself.
body: Mavors is an archaic and poetic form of the name Mars, and Thrace was traditionally his home (Il. 13.301). Lycurgus was a Thracian king who persecuted Dionysus (Il. 6.130-40). Aeneas lands on the coast and founds a town named 'Aeneadae' after himself; there was a real town Aenus (or Aineia) on the Thracian coast which claimed Aeneas as founder, and ancient writers connected the names. Virgil's word 'thwarting fates' (fatis iniquis) warns at once that this foundation is wrong. 'Lord Gradivus, who rules in the Getic fields' (3.35) is again Mars, under an old Roman title of uncertain meaning (perhaps 'the one who marches'), and the Getae were a Thracian tribe.

title: Polydorus: the bleeding myrtle
greek: nam Polydorus ego. hic confixum ferrea texit telorum seges et iaculis increvit acutis
short: Tearing up shoots of myrtle for an altar, Aeneas sees them bleed and hears the voice of Polydorus, Priam's son, murdered here and pierced by spears that took root.
body: Polydorus, Priam's youngest son, had been sent with gold to the Thracian king Polymestor for safekeeping; when Troy fell the king murdered him for the gold. The story is the subject of Euripides' Hecuba, where his ghost speaks the prologue. Virgil turns it into a portent: the spears that killed him have grown into a thicket of cornel and myrtle (myrtle is Venus' plant, and cornel wood was used for spear-shafts), and they bleed when torn. The 'iron harvest of weapons' is a powerful metaphor. The motif of the bleeding, speaking plant was imitated by Dante (Inferno 13, Pier della Vigna), Ariosto and Spenser (Fradubio, Faerie Queene 1.2.30-44). Aeneas' horror is told with lines repeated from Book 2 ('my hair stood up, and the accents faltered on my tongue', 3.48 = 2.774).

title: Auri sacra fames
greek: quid non mortalia pectora cogis, auri sacra fames!
short: Aeneas' outburst against greed for gold became proverbial; sacra here means 'accursed', an old religious sense of the word.
body: The Thracian king broke every bond of duty (fas) for gold. Aeneas exclaims 'to what do you not drive mortal hearts, accursed hunger of gold!' Sacer could mean both 'sacred' and 'accursed', that is, devoted to the gods for destruction; Conington and Page explain the second sense here (compare the legal formula sacer esto, 'let him be accursed'). The theme of gold as the corrupter of loyalty also runs through Dido's story, where Pygmalion murdered Sychaeus 'blind with lust of gold' (1.349). The phrase became a commonplace of moral writing; Dante adapts it in Purgatorio 22.40-41, where Statius says Virgil's line turned him from prodigality.

title: The second funeral of Polydorus
greek: animamque sepulcro condimus et magna supremum voce ciemus
short: The Trojans give Polydorus proper burial with Roman funeral rites: a new mound, altars to the dead, dark fillets and cypress, offerings of milk and blood, and the final call.
body: An unburied or improperly buried person was thought to have no rest (Palinurus pleads for burial in 6.337-83). The Trojans 'bury Polydorus anew': they heap up the mound, set up altars to his Manes (spirits of the dead) decked with dusky fillets and cypress (the tree of mourning), and the women let down their hair in mourning. They pour warm milk and sacrificial blood, offerings to the dead in Roman and Greek cult, and 'lay the spirit to rest' in the tomb. The 'last call' (supremum ciemus) is the conclamatio, the ritual calling of the dead person's name, a final farewell. Page and Conington explain these Roman rites, which Virgil attributes to the Trojans so that Roman customs appear to originate with them.

title: Delos, the floating island
greek: sacra mari colitur medio gratissima tellus Nereidum matri et Neptuno Aegaeo
short: Delos, Apollo's birthplace, once floated about the sea until the god 'the Archer' fixed it between Myconos and Gyaros as a stable home for his mother.
body: According to myth, Delos was a wandering island until it gave refuge to Leto (Latona) when she bore Apollo and Artemis; in gratitude Apollo anchored it (Callimachus, Hymn 4 to Delos; Pindar fr. 33c-d). It was 'most dear to the mother of the Nereids' (Doris) and to Neptune of Aegae, a cult place of Poseidon. 'The Archer god' translates arquitenens, 'bow-holding', an epithet of Apollo. Delos was a famous oracle and religious centre and, in Virgil's day, a great free port. The contrast between the island that once wandered and is now fixed suits the theme of Trojans wandering in search of rest. Myconos and Gyaros are neighbouring islands of the Cyclades.

title: 'Seek out your ancient mother'
greek: Dardanidae duri, quae vos a stirpe parentum prima tulit tellus, eadem vos ubere laeto accipiet reduces. antiquam exquirite matrem
short: Apollo's riddling oracle tells the Trojans to return to the land of their first ancestors; Anchises misreads it as Crete, when the true 'mother' is Italy.
body: Oracles in the Greek tradition are ambiguous, and misreading them is a common motif. The Trojans had two ancestral lines: Teucer, said by some to have come from Crete, and Dardanus, said in Italian tradition to have come from Corythus (Cortona) in Etruria. Anchises remembers Teucer and leads them to Crete. Conington remarks that the enigmatic character of a Greek oracle is well kept. The phrase recalls the Roman story of Lucius Junius Brutus, who interpreted the oracle that whoever first kissed his mother would rule by kissing the earth, the common mother (Livy 1.56.10-12). The promise that the house of Aeneas will rule 'all regions' echoes Iliad 20.307-8, where Poseidon prophesies that Aeneas and his descendants will rule the Trojans.

title: Crete, Mount Ida and Cybele
greek: hinc mater cultrix Cybeli Corybantiaque aera Idaeumque nemus
short: Anchises traces Trojan cults to Crete: the Great Mother Cybele with her lion-drawn chariot, the bronze cymbals of her Corybants, and the name of Mount Ida.
body: Both Crete and the Troad had a Mount Ida, and Anchises argues that the Trojan Ida was named after the Cretan one, where Jupiter was born and hidden. Cybele, the Phrygian 'Great Mother' (Magna Mater), was worshipped with ecstatic music of cymbals and drums by her priests, the Corybantes (often confused or merged with the Cretan Curetes, who clashed their weapons to hide the infant Jupiter's cries). Her chariot was drawn by lions. Romans brought her cult from Asia Minor in 204 BC during the war with Hannibal, and her temple stood on the Palatine near Augustus' house. 'Cybele' here may be the mountain in Phrygia (cultrix Cybeli, 'dweller on Cybelus'); Conington and Page discuss the reading. Gnosus (Knossos) is the chief city of Crete.

anchor: pestilence and a year of death
title: Plague in Crete; Pergamea
greek: corrupto caeli tractu miserandaque venit arboribusque satisque lues et letifer annus
short: The settlement at Pergamea in Crete is struck by plague and the Dog Star's drought: a sign that this, too, is the wrong land.
body: Aeneas founds a city in Crete and calls it Pergamea, after Pergama, the citadel of Troy; he gives laws and allots land, Roman acts of founding (compare Dido at 1.426 and 1.507-8). Plague and drought follow. 'A tainted space of sky' reflects the ancient belief that pestilence arose from corrupted air. Sirius, the Dog Star, whose rising in high summer was associated with heat and disease (Il. 22.26-31), scorches the fields. Plague as a sign of divine displeasure is a very old epic motif (Iliad 1; Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus), and Virgil had written a great plague passage in Georgics 3.478-566. Crete is called 'Curetean' after the Curetes, and Jupiter 'denies' the 'Dictaean fields' (from Mount Dicte) at 3.171.

title: The Penates speak
greek: effigies sacrae divum Phrygiique penates ... visi ante oculos astare iacentis
short: The household gods appear to Aeneas in the moonlight and correct Anchises' error: the true 'ancient mother' is Hesperia, the land of Dardanus.
body: The Penates Aeneas rescued from Troy now repay his care by speaking for Apollo. They appear in clear moonlight through the windows, and Aeneas insists it was not mere sleep (3.173): a 'true' vision, as distinct from a deceptive dream. Their speech repeats Ilioneus' lines on Hesperia from 1.530-3 nearly word for word, and identifies Italy as the home of Dardanus and Iasius, ancestors of the Trojans. 'Ausonia' is a poetic name for Italy, from the Ausones, an ancient people of Campania. Anchises then recalls the 'double descent' of the Trojans (from Teucer and Dardanus) and that Cassandra had foretold Hesperia. Page comments on the repetition from Book 1.

title: Corythus and Dardanus' Italian origin
greek: hinc Dardanus ortus Iasiusque pater ... Corythum terrasque requirat Ausonias
short: Virgil adopts an Italian tradition that Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojans, came from Corythus (Cortona) in Etruria: the Trojans' journey to Italy is a homecoming.
body: In Homer Dardanus is a son of Zeus who founded Dardania (Il. 20.215-18), with no Italian connection. Virgil uses a version, probably current in the late Republic, in which Dardanus came from Italy, from the Etruscan town of Corythus, identified with Cortona; Conington explains that the name probably refers to the place, not to its legendary founder Corythus, Dardanus' father in one story. This makes Aeneas' voyage a nostos, a return home, and gives the Trojans a legitimate claim to Italian land; it is repeated at 7.205-11 and 7.240. Iasius was Dardanus' brother. The innovation shows how Virgil adapts Greek myth to Roman needs.

title: Palinurus, the helmsman
greek: ipse diem noctemque negat discernere caelo nec meminisse viae media Palinurus in unda
short: Palinurus, Aeneas' helmsman, cannot tell day from night in the storm; later he reads the stars for the crossing to Italy, and in Book 5 he is lost overboard.
body: Palinurus is the expert sailor of the fleet. In this storm, which echoes the storm of Book 1 and Odyssey 12.403-25, even he is lost. Later in the book he rises at night, listens for the wind, and observes 'Arcturus, the rainy Hyades and the twin Oxen' and Orion before giving the signal to sail (3.512-20); the stars are the same as in Iopas' song (1.744). His end is one of the poem's most moving episodes: overcome by the god Sleep, he falls into the sea (5.833-71) and his ghost asks Aeneas for burial (6.337-83). Cape Palinuro in southern Italy preserves his name, as Virgil says (6.381).

title: The Harpies and Celaeno
greek: Strophades Graio stant nomine dictae insulae Ionio in magno, quas dira Celaeno Harpyiaeque colunt aliae
short: The Harpies, bird-bodied monsters with girls' faces, foul the Trojans' feasts on the Strophades islands, as they had plagued the blind king Phineus.
body: The Harpies ('snatchers') appear in Homer as storm-winds that carry people off (Od. 20.61-78). In Apollonius of Rhodes (Argonautica 2.178-300) they torment the blind prophet Phineus by snatching and fouling his food until the sons of Boreas drive them away to the Strophades ('Turning Islands', so named because the pursuers turned back there). Virgil makes them hideous: maidens' faces, clawed hands, filth and pallor of hunger. The Trojans had killed cattle they found untended, perhaps the Harpies' own herd, and Celaeno ('the Dark One') calls their attack an outrage. Mackail's 'Stygian waters' refers to the Styx, river of the underworld. Celaeno calls herself 'eldest of the Furies' (Furiarum maxima), a startling identification, since the Furies (Dirae) are underworld avengers.

title: The prophecy of the eaten tables
greek: ambesas subigat malis absumere mensas
short: Celaeno curses the Trojans: they will not found their city until hunger makes them eat their tables. The prophecy is harmlessly fulfilled at 7.107-29.
body: Celaeno's curse sounds terrible, but it turns out to be a riddle. In Book 7, after landing in Latium, the Trojans eat their meal off flat cakes of bread used as plates, and then eat the 'tables' too; Iulus jokes 'Look, we are eating even our tables!' (7.116), and Aeneas recognises the fulfilment. There is a notable inconsistency: in Book 7 Aeneas attributes the prophecy to Anchises, not to Celaeno (7.122-7). Helenus also refers to it at 3.394-5. Commentators explain the discrepancy as one of the signs that Virgil had not finished revising the poem. The motif of the tables came from earlier tradition; Dionysius of Halicarnassus (1.55) says an oracle at Dodona or a Sibyl foretold it.

title: Games on the Actian shore
greek: Actiaque Iliacis celebramus litora ludis
short: The Trojans hold 'Ilian games' at Actium, where Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC and founded the Actian Games: myth anticipates Augustan history.
body: Actium, a promontory on the Ambracian Gulf in western Greece, was the site of Octavian's decisive naval victory in 31 BC. He enlarged the temple of Apollo there, founded the city of Nicopolis ('Victory City') and established games, the Actia, held every four years. Virgil makes Aeneas hold Trojan games on the same shore, a pointed anticipation that links the founder to the refounder of Rome; Actium is also the centre of the shield of Aeneas (8.675-713). Page notes a geographical confusion: at 3.274-6 the Trojans land near Leucate on Leucas, but the 'Actian shore' is a little further north. Mackail's 'Apollo dreaded of sailors' is the temple of Apollo on the Leucadian cliff.

title: Andromache at Hector's cenotaph
greek: falsi Simoentis ad undam libabat cineri Andromache manisque vocabat Hectoreum ad tumulum, viridi quem caespite inanem
short: At Buthrotum Aeneas finds Andromache, Hector's widow, pouring offerings at an empty tomb by a river she has renamed Simois: a life lived among memories.
body: Andromache, captive of Pyrrhus after the fall of Troy, is now the wife of Helenus, another Trojan captive, who rules part of Epirus after Pyrrhus' death. Aeneas finds her performing funeral rites at a cenotaph (an empty tomb, inanem) for Hector by a stream called after Troy's river Simois, 'false Simois'. Her two altars may be for Hector and Astyanax. Her first question, whether Aeneas is alive or a ghost, and 'where is Hector?', show a mind fixed in the past. The scene, with its replica Troy, poses one of Virgil's central questions: whether the Trojans should rebuild Troy or found something new. Euripides' Andromache told of her life with Neoptolemus.

title: Polyxena: 'happy above all others'
greek: o felix una ante alias Priameia virgo, hostilem ad tumulum Troiae sub moenibus altis iussa mori
short: Andromache envies Polyxena, Priam's daughter sacrificed at Achilles' tomb, because she died before becoming a Greek's slave-concubine as Andromache did.
body: Polyxena was sacrificed to the ghost of Achilles at his tomb after the fall of Troy, a story dramatised in Euripides' Hecuba. Andromache calls her 'happy' because she never 'bore the lot' (the drawing of lots by which captive women were assigned) or entered a victor's bed. Conington notes that the phrase 'under high Troy town' is used loosely, since Euripides places the death in the Thracian Chersonese, while Virgil follows a version that put Achilles' tomb on the Sigean promontory. Andromache then tells how Pyrrhus married Hermione, Helen's daughter, and passed her on to Helenus 'a bondwoman to a bondman', and how Orestes killed Pyrrhus at his ancestral altars (an ironic parallel to Priam's death).

title: Buthrotum's 'little Troy'
greek: procedo et parvam Troiam simulataque magnis Pergama et arentem Xanthi cognomine rivum agnosco, Scaeaeque amplector limina portae
short: Helenus has built a miniature Troy, with a dry brook called Xanthus and a Scaean gate: a poignant copy that shows the danger of living in the past.
body: Buthrotum (modern Butrint, Albania) was a town in Epirus which in Virgil's day had a Roman colony founded under Caesar and Augustus. Helenus' city is a replica of Troy: 'Pergama made like the great ones', a 'dry brook' named after the Xanthus (Troy's river, also called Scamander), and a 'Scaean gate', which Aeneas embraces. The diminutives and the drying river suggest something small and lifeless. Many readers take the episode as a lesson: Aeneas' Troy must not be a copy but a new beginning, as Juno finally demands at 12.819-28, when Jupiter agrees that the Trojan name will disappear. Aeneas' farewell speech (3.493-505) admits that Helenus and Andromache have rest, while he is called 'from fate to fate'.

title: Helenus, Trojan prophet
greek: Troiugena, interpres divum, qui numina Phoebi, qui tripodas, Clarii lauros, qui sidera sentis et volucrum linguas et praepetis omina pennae
short: Helenus, Priam's son, is a seer skilled in every form of divination: Apollo's tripods and laurels, the stars, bird-cries and the flight of birds.
body: In the Iliad Helenus is 'the best of augurs' (Il. 6.76). Aeneas' address lists the methods of ancient divination: inspiration by Apollo (the tripod of Delphi and the laurels of Claros, an oracle of Apollo near Colophon), astrology (the stars), the cries of birds (oscines) and their flight (alites, 'birds of prosperous flight', praepetes). These were all practised or known at Rome, where augury from birds was an official public institution. Helenus' prophecy (3.374-462) is the longest in Book 3 and the guide for the rest of the voyage; but he says that the Fates and Juno forbid him to tell everything, and he does not predict Anchises' death (3.712-13). Andromache's farewell gifts to Ascanius, recalling her dead son Astyanax, follow.

title: Helenus' prophecy: the route to Italy
greek: longa procul longis via dividit invia terris
short: Helenus warns that the nearest coast of Italy is held by Greeks, that they must sail round Sicily, avoid Scylla and Charybdis, placate Juno and consult the Sibyl at Cumae.
body: Helenus' speech is the Virgilian counterpart of Circe's and Tiresias' instructions to Odysseus (Od. 11.100-37; 12.37-141). The Italian coast near Epirus is full of Greek settlers: Locrians from Narycum, Idomeneus in the Sallentine plain, and Philoctetes ('the Meliboean captain', from Meliboea in Thessaly) at Petelia. The Trojans must go round Sicily ('the Trinacrian wave', Trinacria being the three-cornered island), past 'Aeaean Circe's isle' (Circe's home Aeaea, located in Italy at Monte Circeo) and the 'infernal pools' of Avernus. Conington and Page note that some predictions do not quite match what happens. The repetition of 'one thing ... one thing for all' (unum illud ... unum pro cunctis) emphasises the command to worship Juno.

title: The white sow and her thirty piglets
greek: litoreis ingens inventa sub ilicibus sus triginta capitum fetus enixa iacebit, alba, solo recubans, albi circum ubera nati
short: Helenus' sign for the city's site: a huge white sow with thirty white young by a river, seen in Book 8 and linked with Alba Longa.
body: The omen of the sow was an old part of the Aeneas legend, connected with Lavinium, where Varro says a bronze sow was shown, and with Alba Longa ('the long white'), whose name was explained by the white sow (alba). The thirty piglets were said to mean the thirty years before Ascanius founded Alba, or the thirty towns of the Latin League. Aeneas sees the sow at 8.42-85 on the bank of the Tiber, where the river-god Tiberinus repeats this prophecy almost word for word (8.43-5), and he sacrifices it to Juno (8.84-5). Dionysius of Halicarnassus (1.56-7) gives another version in which the sow runs from the sacrifice and leads Aeneas to the site of Lavinium.

title: Sacrificing with veiled head
greek: purpureo velare comas adopertus amictu, ne qua inter sanctos ignis in honore deorum hostilis facies occurrat et omina turbet
short: Helenus explains the Roman custom of sacrificing with the head covered (capite velato), unlike the Greek bare-headed rite, so that no hostile sight can spoil the omens.
body: Romans prayed and sacrificed with a fold of the toga drawn over the head (capite velato), whereas Greeks sacrificed bareheaded; the custom was so characteristic that Augustus is shown veiled in the act of sacrifice on the Ara Pacis and on statues. Virgil gives the custom a Trojan origin: Helenus prescribes it so that no hostile face should be seen during worship and spoil the omens. Servius tells a related aetiological story, that Aeneas covered his head while sacrificing when the Greek Diomedes appeared; Page discusses the custom. The Trojans follow the rule as soon as they land in Italy (3.543-7), veiled in 'Phrygian garments', and sacrifice to 'Juno of Argos' as Helenus had commanded.

anchor: On the right Scylla keeps guard
title: Scylla and Charybdis
greek: dextrum Scylla latus, laevum implacata Charybdis obsidet
short: At the Strait of Messina, Scylla, a monster with a girl's upper body and a sea-dragon's tail ringed with dogs, faces the whirlpool Charybdis: the Trojans must sail around.
body: In Homer (Od. 12.73-126, 234-59) Scylla is a six-headed monster in a cave who snatches six of Odysseus' men, and Charybdis a whirlpool that swallows the sea three times a day. The pair were located in antiquity at the Strait of Messina, between Italy and Sicily, which Helenus explains was formed when the land was torn apart (behind this lies a Greek etymology of the town Rhegium from rhegnymi, 'break'). Virgil's Scylla follows later Greek art and poetry: a beautiful maiden above, a sea-monster below, with wolves or dogs around her waist and dolphins' tails. Aeneas had mentioned both dangers in his speech at 1.200-1. Unlike Odysseus, Aeneas is told to avoid the passage altogether by sailing round Pachynus, Sicily's southern cape; at 3.554-69 the fleet nearly meets Charybdis anyway.

anchor: marks down her words on leaves
title: The Sibyl of Cumae and her leaves
greek: insanam vatem aspicies, quae rupe sub ima fata canit foliisque notas et nomina mandat
short: Helenus describes the raving Sibyl of Cumae, whose leaf-written oracles scatter in the wind; Aeneas must make her speak aloud. She guides him in Book 6.
body: Cumae, near Naples, the oldest Greek colony in Italy, was the seat of a Sibyl, an inspired prophetess of Apollo. Rome possessed the Sibylline Books, collections of oracles said to have been bought by King Tarquin from a Sibyl, kept on the Capitol and consulted in crises; Augustus had them recopied and moved to his new temple of Apollo on the Palatine. Helenus' description of verses written on leaves that are scattered by the draught from the door explains why visitors 'depart without counsel'. Aeneas remembers the warning and asks her to speak, not write (6.74-6). Avernus is a crater lake near Cumae, believed to be an entrance to the underworld. Page and Conington explain the details.

title: The omen of the four white horses
greek: quattuor hic, primum omen, equos in gramine vidi tondentis campum late, candore nivali
short: The first sign in Italy is four white horses: Anchises reads it as war (horses are armed for battle) but also hope of peace (they can be yoked together).
body: Anchises' reading is a model of Roman augural interpretation: one sign carrying a double message. 'War dost thou carry, land of our sojourn' (bellum, o terra hospita, portas) foretells the war in Latium (Books 7-12); horses also draw the chariot and plough in concord, so there is hope of peace (spes et pacis). Four white horses also drew the chariot of a Roman general in a triumph, which some readers see as a further hint. The hospitable land (terra hospita) will become hostile. Conington and Page discuss the omen.

title: Achemenides, the Greek castaway
greek: sum patria ex Ithaca, comes infelicis Ulixi, nomine Achaemenides
short: A Greek companion of Ulysses left behind in the Cyclops' land begs the Trojans for rescue; they accept the enemy suppliant, and he joins their voyage.
body: Achemenides is Virgil's invention (or at least not known earlier). He links the Aeneid's narrative to Odyssey 9: he was abandoned when Ulysses' men fled Polyphemus' cave, and he retells the blinding of the Cyclops from a survivor's point of view. Thematically he is the counterpart of Sinon in Book 2: both are Greeks who come to Trojans as suppliants with a pitiful story, but Sinon lies and Achemenides tells the truth. The Trojans, led by Anchises, who gives him his hand as 'visible pledge', show pity and are proved right. His name has been connected with the Persian royal Achaemenids, and his father Adamastus is otherwise unknown. Conington's notes discuss his role.

title: Polyphemus: monstrum horrendum
greek: monstrum horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum
short: The blinded Cyclops appears on the mountain: one of the most famous lines in Virgil piles up four adjectives and ends with the loss of his eye.
body: Polyphemus, the Cyclops blinded by Odysseus (Od. 9), comes down to the sea to wash his bleeding eye socket. The line monstrum horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum is heavy with spondees and elisions, which imitate his size and clumsy movement; it is often cited as an example of sound echoing sense. The blinded giant was compared to 'an Argolic shield or the lamp of the moon' (3.637) by Achemenides, describing his single eye. The other Cyclopes gather on the shore like tall oaks or cypresses, a 'dreadful consistory' (concilium horrendum). Polyphemus also had a gentler life in pastoral poetry as the lover of Galatea (Theocritus 11), and Virgil touches on this in his care for his sheep, 'his single delight and solace in ill'.

title: Alpheus and Arethusa
greek: Alpheum fama est huc Elidis amnem occultas egisse vias subter mare, qui nunc ore, Arethusa, tuo Siculis confunditur undis
short: The river Alpheus of Elis in Greece was believed to flow under the sea to rise in the fountain Arethusa at Syracuse, mingling with the nymph he loved.
body: Ortygia is the island at the heart of Syracuse in Sicily (not the Ortygia that is another name for Delos, used at 3.124 and 3.143). The fountain Arethusa there was believed to be fed by the Peloponnesian river Alpheus, which flows past Olympia; in myth the river-god pursued the nymph Arethusa, who fled under the sea to Sicily (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.572-641). Ancient writers reported that objects thrown into the Alpheus at Olympia reappeared at Syracuse. Virgil had invoked Arethusa as a Muse of pastoral poetry at Eclogue 10.1-6, and Conington refers to his note there. The coastal catalogue that follows (Helorus, Pachynus, Camarina, Gela, Acragas, Selinus, Lilybaeum) traces Sicily's southern shore in order.

title: Camarina: 'do not move Camarina'
greek: et fatis numquam concessa moveri apparet Camarina procul
short: Camarina, a Greek city in Sicily, was told by an oracle not to drain its marsh; it did, and enemies crossed the dry ground: 'move not Camarina' became a proverb.
body: The story, preserved by Servius and Greek proverb-collections, is that the people of Camarina asked Apollo whether to drain the pestilential marsh beside their city; the oracle answered 'Do not move Camarina' (me kinei Kamarinan). They drained it anyway, and enemies crossed the dried marsh and took the city. The proverb was used for stirring up trouble unnecessarily. Virgil alludes to it in a single phrase, typical of his learned, Hellenistic manner. Many manuscripts and some interpretations are discussed by Conington; Page summarises the coastal journey. 'Palm-girt Selinus' refers to the wild palms on that coast, 'Acragas' is Agrigento, once famous for racehorses.

title: The death of Anchises at Drepanum
greek: hic pelagi tot tempestatibus actus heu genitorem, omnis curae casusque levamen, amitto Anchisen
short: Book 3 ends with Anchises' death at Drepanum in western Sicily, told in a few lines; neither Helenus nor Celaeno had foretold it. Aeneas then falls silent.
body: Drepanum (modern Trapani) is on the western tip of Sicily. Anchises, the religious guide of Book 3, dies there, and Aeneas grieves in direct address ('Here thou, dear lord, abandonest me'). In some earlier versions of the legend Anchises reached Italy; Virgil places his death before the arrival in Carthage, so that Aeneas comes to Dido without his father's counsel. The anniversary of his death is the occasion for the funeral games of Book 5, and Aeneas meets his shade in the underworld in Book 6. The closing lines frame the whole narrative of Books 2-3: 'Thus lord Aeneas ... retold alone the divine doom', and he 'made an end' (conticuit, the same verb that opened Book 2, conticuere omnes, 'all fell silent').
